rows.speaker: الإمام الأسيوطي
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti derives the term from knowledge when the worlds are understood generally, and from a sign when the term is taken in its broader sense.
rows.anchor: هو مشتق من العلم وعلى القول بالعموم من العلامة

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One reported view limits the worlds to jinn and humans, appealing to the description of the Messenger as a warner to all worlds.
rows.anchor: وقيل هم الجن والإنس لقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: جعفر الصادق
rows.claim: A view transmitted from Jaʿfar al-Ṣādiq limits the worlds to humans; al-Alusi suggests humans are the central object of religious duties and messengers.
rows.anchor: وهو المنقول عن جعفر الصادق والمأخوذ من بحر أهل البيت ورب البيت أدرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humanity is a concentrated summary of created things, and reflection on the self reveals the Creator's greatness; the apt reading here remains universal.
rows.anchor: ولعل الوجه فيه الإشارة إلى أن الإنسان هو المقصود بالذات من التكليف بالحلال والحرام

rows.speaker: علي بن أبي طالب
rows.claim: An aphorism attributed to the Gate of Knowledge says that the human being contains the greater world and carries both remedy and illness within.
rows.anchor: دواؤك فيك وما تبصر وداؤك منك وما تشعر وتزعم أنك جرم صغير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi prefers the universal sense because the worlds are innumerable and God's nurturing encompasses every existing thing, both celestial and earthly.
rows.anchor: والمناسب للمقام هنا العموم والعوالم كثيرة لا تحصيها الأرقام

rows.speaker: بعض الأخبار
rows.claim: A report says God created one hundred thousand lamps suspended from the Throne, with the heavens, earth, Paradise, and Hell in one lamp; only God knows the rest.
rows.anchor: وروى في بعض الأخبار أن الله تعالى خلق مائة ألف قنديل وعلقها بالعرش

rows.speaker: كعب الأحبار
rows.claim: Kaʿb al-Aḥbār says only God can count the number of worlds.
rows.anchor: وقال كعب الأحبار لا يحصى عدد العالمين إلا الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every contingent being depends on God's continual nurturing for existence and persistence; sustaining it also means keeping all its possible impediments absent.
rows.anchor: وما من ذرة من ذرات العوالم إلا وهي حيطة تربيته سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A mystic's saying contrasts God's care for the servant with the servant's lax service: God tends him as though no other servant existed, though God owns countless others.
rows.anchor: أحسن قول بعض العارفين أنه تعالى يملك عبادا غيرك وأنت ليس لك رب سواه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The masculine sound plural can denote paucity despite the many worlds, underscoring that all are insignificant beside God's majesty; Arabic usage can also allow either number.
rows.anchor: تنبيها على أن العوالم وإن كثرت قليلة بل أقل من القليل في جنب عظمة الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rabb names the station of divine lordship that calls for the created objects required by attributes such as knowledge, power, will, and hearing.
rows.anchor: إلى حضرة الربوبية التي هي مقام العارفين وهي اسم للمرتبة المقتضية للأسماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names beneath Rabb include attributes shared in some respect between Creator and creation and active names exclusive to God; the latter belong under Malik.
rows.anchor: والأسماء التي تحت أسم الرب هي الأسماء المشتركة بين الحق والخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahman is more comprehensive than Rabb because it gathers every exalted divine attribute, whether exclusive to God or related to creation.
rows.anchor: وأما الفرق بين الرب والرحمن فهو أن الرحمن عندهم أسم لمرتبة أختصت بجميع الأوصاف العلية الألهية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Allah signifies the all-encompassing divine essence and highest level; below it are oneness, mercifulness, lordship, and sovereignty, while absolute divine uniqueness has no manifestation of created qualities.
rows.anchor: فهو أسم لمرتبة ذاتية جامعة وفلك محيط بالحقائق

rows.speaker: أرباب الظاهر
rows.claim: Outward scholars explain frequent supplication with Rabb as fitting because a petitioner seeks what seems beneficial for personal nurture and care.
rows.anchor: وقال أرباب الظاهر الداعي لا يطلب إلا ما يظنه صلاحا لحاله وتربية لنفسه

rows.speaker: ساداتنا الصوفية
rows.claim: Sufi masters say the appropriate divine name in prayer changes with the seeker's spiritual state and whether the experience is one of differentiation or union.
rows.anchor: وعند ساداتنا الصوفية قدس الله تعالى أسرارهم يختلف الكلام بإختلاف المقام فرقا وجمعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The primordial spirits first heard and affirmed God's lordship, so they call on Him by the first name through which they recognized and pledged themselves to Him.
rows.anchor: فهم ينادونه سبحانه بأول أسم قررهم به فأقروا وأخذ به عليهم العهد

rows.speaker: الشيخ الأكبر
rows.claim: Ibn ʿArabi describes the universal Spirit, initially unaware of its origin, as journeying inward until God showed it its secrets and taught it to recognize Him as Lord, while reserving divinity to Himself.
rows.anchor: مما حاصله أن الله تعالى لما أوجد الكلمة المعبر عنها بالروح الكلي إيجاد إبداع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opening the Fatiha's descriptions with Lord of the worlds suits the Prophet's mission as a profound act of nurturing humanity and hints at compassion for all people.
rows.anchor: ويعلم منه إشارة سر إفتتاح الأوصاف في الفاتحة برب العالمين

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: A reading attributed to Zayd ibn ʿAli puts Rabb al-ʿalamin in the accusative; al-Alusi finds the first grammatical explanation, an implied praise or mention verb, most apparent.
rows.anchor: وقد قرء رب العالمين بالنصب ونسب ذلك إلى زيد بن علي رضي الله تعالى عنهما

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: One analysis treats the accusative as an adjective cut off from its antecedent, supplying an implied verb such as I praise or I mention; an objection about the following adjective is answered by taking Rahman as apposition.
rows.anchor: فقيل نصب على القطع ويقدر العامل هنا أمدح للمقام أو أذكر

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abu Hayyan rejects deriving the accusative from the earlier praise merely by attraction, arguing that this mechanism belongs to coordination; al-Alusi disputes that objection using grammatical authorities.
rows.anchor: وليس على التوهم كما توهم أبو حيان فضعفه بزعمه أنه من خصائص العطف

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another analysis supplies the earlier word al-ḥamd as the governing verb; objections concern the definite verbal noun's government and an intervening predicate, both answered by grammarians.
rows.anchor: وقيل بفعل مقدر دل عليه الحمد وليس على التوهم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Other proposed parses take Rabb as a vocative or a past-tense verb, but al-Alusi finds the vocative unclear and the verbal reading syntactically remote.
rows.anchor: وقيل بالنداء ولا يخفى ما فيه من اللبس والفصل والإلتفات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi considers an accusative absolute construction the strongest and nearly compelled by the apparent wording.
rows.anchor: والمناسب المناسبة وأهون الأمور عندي أولها بل يكاد يقطع الظاهر بالقطع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After stating God's universal nurturing, the verse declares His immense mercy; the majority read both names in the genitive, while Zayd, Abu al-ʿAliya, Ibn al-Sumayqa, and ʿIsa ibn ʿAmr read them accusatively, and several others raise them.
rows.anchor: والجمهور على خفضهما ونصبهما زيد وأبو العالية وإبن السميقع وعيسى بن عمرو

rows.speaker: بعض ساداتنا
rows.claim: Some Sufi masters infer from repeating the two names here and in the basmala that the basmala is not a verse of the Fatiha; al-Alusi calls the inference weak because each occurrence has a distinct purpose.
rows.anchor: وأستدل بعض ساداتنا بتكرارهما على أن البسملة ليست آية من الفاتحة وليس بالقوى

rows.speaker: الإمام الرازي
rows.claim: Al-Razi explains the repetition as stressing mercy more than other matters, then balancing hope with the warning that God is Master of Judgment Day; al-Alusi objects that divinity is repeated too.
rows.anchor: قال الإمام الرازي قدس سره في بيان حكمة التكرار التقدير كأنه قيل له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi's Sufi reading makes Rahman and Rahim a detailed account of Rabb's general nurturing: care may be mediated or immediate, and mediated care may involve hardship or pure kindness.
rows.anchor: وعندي بمسلك صوفي أن ذكر الرحمن الرحيم تفصيل من وجه لما في رب العالمين من الإجمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rahman points to nurturing through intermediaries and across the worlds, including mercy mixed with painful medicine; Rahim points to direct nurturing through divine words as pure blessing for the fully happy.
rows.anchor: فالرحمن يشير إلى التربية بالوسائط وغيرها في عالمه والرحيم يشير إلى التربية بلا واسطة في كلماته

rows.speaker: عاصم والكسائي وخلف ويعقوب
rows.claim: They read Mālik with a long first vowel and genitive ending; this is the reading of the Ten except Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr, and is also reported from many early Muslims.
rows.anchor: قرأ مالك كفاعل مخفوضا عاصم والكسائي وخلف في إختياره ويعقوب

rows.speaker: باقي السبعة وزيد وأبو الدرداء وإبن عمرو والمسور
rows.claim: They read Malik without the long vowel in the genitive, as did many Companions and Successors.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ملك كفعل بالخفض أيضا باقي السبعة وزيد وأبو الدرداء

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة وعاصم الجحدري
rows.claim: They read Malik on the pattern of sahl; the reading is also transmitted by al-Jaʿfi and ʿAbd al-Warith from Abu ʿAmr, and described as a Bakr ibn Waʾil dialect.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ملك على وزن سهل أبو هريرة وعاصم الجحدري ورواها الجعفي

rows.speaker: أحمد بن صالح عن ورش عن نافع
rows.claim: A reading transmitted by Aḥmad ibn Ṣāliḥ from Warsh from Nāfiʿ lengthens the second syllable in Maliki.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ملكي بإشباع كثرة الكاف أحمد بن صالح عن ورش عن نافع

rows.speaker: أبو عثمان والشعبي وعطية
rows.claim: They read Malik on the pattern of ʿajul.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ملك على وزن عجل أبو عثمان والشعبي وعطية

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك وأبو نوفل عمرو بن مسلم البصري
rows.claim: They read Malik with the kaf in the accusative and no alif.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أنس بن مالك وأبو نوفل عمرو بن مسلم البصري ملك يوم الدين

rows.speaker: سعد بن أبي وقاص وعائشة
rows.claim: They read the same form with the kaf raised.
rows.anchor: وقرأ كذلك إلا أنه رفع الكاف سعد بن أبي وقاص وعائشة

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة وأبو حيوة وجبير بن مطعم
rows.claim: They read Malaka as a past-tense verb and put yawm in the accusative; Ibn ʿAṭiyya also attributes this reading to ʿAli, al-Ḥasan, and Yaḥya ibn Yaʿmar.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ملك فعلا ماضيا أبو حنيفة على ما قيل وأبو حيوة وجبير بن مطعم

rows.speaker: الأعمش وإبن السميقع وعثمان بن أبي سليمان
rows.claim: They read Mālika with the word in the accusative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مالك بالنصب الأعمش أيضا وإبن السميقع وعثمان بن أبي سليمان

rows.speaker: عمر بن عبدالعزيز وأبو صالح السمان
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes the accusative reading of Mālik to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and Abu Ṣāliḥ al-Sammān.
rows.anchor: وذكر إبن عطية أنها قراءة عمر بن عبدالعزيز وأبي صالح السمان

rows.speaker: اليماني
rows.claim: Al-Yamānī, through Ibn ʿĀṣim, reads Mālik in the accusative with nunation.
rows.anchor: وروى إبن عاصم عن اليماني مالكا بالنصب والتنوين

rows.speaker: خلف وإبن هشام وأبي عبيد وأبي حاتم
rows.claim: A reading attributed to Khalaf, Ibn Hishām, Abu ʿUbayd, and Abu Ḥātim raises the kaf and nunates Mālik, with yawm in the accusative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مالك برفع الكاف والتنوين ورويت عن خلف وإبن هشام وأبي عبيد

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة وأبو حيوة وعمر بن عبدالعزيز
rows.claim: They read Mālik with a raised kaf and genitive yawm; al-Lawāmiʿ attributes this to Shaddād al-ʿUqaylī al-Baṣrī as well.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مالك يوم بالرفع والإضافة أبو هريرة وأبو حيوة وعمر بن عبدالعزيز

rows.speaker: أبو هريرة وأبو رجاء العطاردي
rows.claim: They read Malīk on the intensive pattern faʿīl.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مليك كفعيل أبو هريرة في رواية وأبو رجاء العطاردي

rows.speaker: يحيى بن يعمر وأيوب السختياني
rows.claim: They read Mālik with strong imāla; Qutayba reports a middle degree from al-Kisāʾī, though Abu ʿAli al-Fārisi says nobody used imāla, and an alif-lengthened form is also cited.
rows.anchor: وقرأ مالك بالإمالة البليغة يحيى بن يعمر وأيوب السختياني

rows.speaker: بعض اللغويين
rows.claim: Some lexicographers relate Mālik and Malik to holding or binding, citing the phrase for kneading dough and a poetic line in which the hand grips something.
rows.anchor: وهما راجعان إلى الملك وهو الشد والربط ومنه ملك العجين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two mutawatir readings, Mālik and Malik, are both brilliant pillars of the recitation tradition.
rows.anchor: والمتواتر منها قراءة مالك وملك فهما نيرا سواريها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari prefers Malik because it is the reading of the two Holy Cities, fits verses about sovereignty, has broader scope, and avoids alleged repetition with Rabb; al-Kashshaf supports him.
rows.anchor: وملك هو الإختيار لأنه قراءة أهل الحرمين ولقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi rejects preference based on the readers of the two Holy Cities: every famous reading is mutawatir, so the geographic pedigree of transmitters cannot rank them.
rows.anchor: لأن قراءة أهل الحرمين لا تدل على الرجحان لأنه لو سلم كون أوائلهم أعلم بالقرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument from God's exclusive sovereignty on Judgment Day must be weighed against the verse saying no soul will own anything for another then, which implies God's ownership.
rows.anchor: فإنه سبحانه أراد باليوم يوم القيامة وهو يوم الدين ونفى المالكية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The use of Malik with people elsewhere does not establish a distinction here: if that passage said Mālik al-nās, it would repeat Rabb al-nās, whereas the Fatiha has a different context.
rows.anchor: فلأن ما في الناس مغاير لما هنا لأن مالك الناس لو كان هناك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that Malik is more general and milk more specific is not the apparent linguistic rule; examples show ownership and kingship overlap in both directions.
rows.anchor: فلأن ما أدعاه من أن الملك بضم الميم يعم والملك بالكسر يخص خلاف الظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The alleged redundancy with Rabb fails because al-Jawhari says Rabb can also mean king, so the two readings face the same objection.
rows.anchor: وأما خامسا فبأن التكرار الذي زعمه صاحب الكشف قد كشف أمره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description Mālik al-Mulk supports the opposite argument: the Owner is more comprehensive because sovereignty itself is placed within His ownership.
rows.anchor: فلأن الدليل الأخير الذي ساقه لك أن تقلبه بأنه تعالى وصف ذاته بالمالكية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi sees no practical fruit in preferring either reading: Mālik and Malik are equally strong divine attributes, and the grammatical analogy used to distinguish them is irrelevant.
rows.anchor: وعندي لا ثمرة للخلاف والقراءتان فرسا رهان ولا فرق بين المالك والملك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though he cannot establish a decisive preference, al-Alusi himself reads Mālik for its extra ten rewards and because ownership evokes wider mercy and hope for sinners than kingship.
rows.anchor: إلا أني أقرأ كالكسائي مالك لأحظى بزيادة عشر حسنات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word yawm can mean sunrise to sunset conventionally, dawn to sunset in Sunni legal usage, or any span of time; Judgment Day is its established religious sense.
rows.anchor: في العرف عبارة عما بين طلوع الشمس وغروبها من الزمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dīn principally means recompense; the transmitted saying from the Prophet states that goodness does not perish, sin is not forgotten, and the Requiter does not die, so one is repaid as one acts.
rows.anchor: ومنه الحديث المرسل عن أبي قلابة رضي الله تعالى عنه قال قال رسول الله

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A reported distinction makes dīn recompense measured to the agent's deed, while jazāʾ is broader; another restricts dīn to a proportionate, deserved recompense.
rows.anchor: وقيل فرق بينهما فإن الدين ما كان بقدر فعل المجازي والجزاء أعم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi prefers treating dīn and jazāʾ as synonymous, so the phrase means the Day of Recompense, supported by verses describing each soul's repayment for its deeds.
rows.anchor: والأرجح عندي أن الدين والجزاء بمعنى فيوم الدين هو يوم الجزاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The genitive attachment of Mālik to yawm uses a permitted extension of a flexible temporal noun, which can behave like a direct object without ceasing to mark time.
rows.anchor: وإضافة مالك إلى يوم على التوسع وقد قال النحاة الظرف إما متصرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An extended temporal object can make an intransitive verb take one object, a verb with one object take two, or one with two take three; extension to a fourth object is generally denied.
rows.anchor: وإذا توسع في الظرف فإن كان فعله غير متعد تعدى وإن كان متعديا إلى واحد

rows.speaker: إبن السراج
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sarrāj is reported to allow a verb already taking three objects to extend to a fourth, though the usual grammar denies this.
rows.anchor: وحكى إبن السراج جوازه والتوسع هذا تجوز حكمي في النسبة الظرفية

rows.speaker: الرضي
rows.claim: Al-Raḍī says grammarians agree that a temporal noun retains the same time meaning whether it is used narrowly as an adverb or extended into an object-like construction.
rows.anchor: أتفقوا على أن معنى الظرف متوسعا فيه وغير متوسع فيه سواء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The meaning is that God owns all affairs on Judgment Day; this ownership is eternal whether treated as an essential attribute or, in Maturidi theology, an active attribute.
rows.anchor: والمعنى مالك الأمر كله في يوم الدين وهذا ثابت له سبحانه أزلا وأبدا

rows.speaker: الزركشي
rows.claim: Al-Zarkashi reports that even Ashʿaris may call God creator and provider before creation and provision exist, and regard the descriptions as literal despite the later arising of acts.
rows.anchor: بل قال الزركشي من الأشاعرة في إطلاق الخالق والرزاق ونحوهما في حقه

rows.speaker: العلامة البيضاوي
rows.claim: On an alternative reading as Malik of affairs on that day, al-Bayḍāwī's explanation implies a dependent metaphor of divine sovereignty.
rows.anchor: ففي الآية إستعارة تبعية كما يفهمه كلام العلامة البيضاوي في تفسيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's ownership is not constrained by ordinary temporal succession: for Him morning, evening, past, and future collapse to one point, with expressions calibrated to human understanding.
rows.anchor: ليس عند ربك صباح ولا مساء وهو سبحانه ليس بزماني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A familiar objection says one cannot own a day that does not yet exist; replies treat Judgment as certain and present, or reason that death is already one's personal resurrection.
rows.anchor: ومن هنا يستنبط جواب للسؤال المشهور بأن المالك لا يكون مالكا للشيء إلأ إذا كان موجودا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For theologians who regard time as nonexistent, the difficulty remains; it can be answered by taking ownership of the day as a metonym for owning everything within it, without requiring literal ownership to be possible.
rows.anchor: إلا أن يقال يجعل الكلام كناية عن كونه مالكا للأمر كله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading Malik avoids the future-day objection if it is a descriptive or frozen noun, but a hyperbolic active participle raises the same issue as Mālik.
rows.anchor: وأنت إذا قرأت ملك تسلم من هذا القيل إن جعلته صفة مشبهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase Day of Recompense suits the rhyme and is broader than Day of Resurrection, spanning every stage of the afterlife and even, by extension, the first creation.
rows.anchor: قال مالك يوم الدين ولم يقل يوم القيامة مراعاة للفاصلة وترجيحا للعموم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Since dīn can also mean obedience or religious law, some understand the day as the day of recompense belonging to obedience or established by religion, with an implied noun in either reading.
rows.anchor: كالطاعة والشريعة فتذهب نفس السامع إلى كل مذهب سائغ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Specifying Judgment Day despite God's ownership of all things either magnifies that day or contrasts apparent worldly human sovereignty with its complete disappearance in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وتخصيص اليوم بالإضافة مع أنه تعالى مالك وملك جميع الأشياء في كل الأوقات والأيام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On that day all creatures assemble and God's attributes of beauty and majesty appear in their fullest manifestation, revealing His ownership of individuals and the whole together.
rows.anchor: وأيضا هنالك يجتمع الأولون والآخرون ويقوم الروح والملائكة صفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The descriptions close by pointing to resurrection, just as Lord of the worlds opened with origination; they explain the prior praise and prepare for the prayer that follows.
rows.anchor: وإنما ختم سبحانه هذه الأوصاف بهذا الوصف إشارة إلى الإعادة كما أفتتح بما يشير إلى الإبداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The five names answer four grounds for praising someone: inherent perfection, past beneficence, hoped-for future kindness, and fear of power; God encompasses them all.
rows.anchor: أن الذي يحمده الناس ويعظمونه إنما يكون حمده وتعظيمه لأحد أمور أربعة

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: An argument for rational gratitude before revelation says the verse establishes God's praiseworthiness through creation, mercy, and future judgment; al-Alusi replies that this proof itself is scriptural, not rational.
rows.anchor: ومن الناس من أستدل كما قال الإمام على وجوب اشكر عقلا قبل مجيء الشرع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says deriving the duty of gratitude from God's own revealed declaration only proves it through revelation, so it cannot establish a pre-revelation rational duty.
rows.anchor: فهو سمعي لا عقلي فالمستدل به كناطح صخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Sufi anthropology maps the five divine names to the human's angelic intellect, devilish, predatory, animal, and dense bodily dimensions, with cited verses illustrating the correspondences.
rows.anchor: فالإنسان بدن ونفس شيطانية ونفس سبعية ونفس بهيمية وجوهر ملكي عقلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The five manifestations yield bodily worship, the devilish soul's request for help, the predatory soul's request for guidance, the animal soul's request for uprightness, and the holy spirit's request to join purified spirits; the pillars of Islam likewise correspond to the five names.
rows.anchor: وآثار هذا التجلي طاعة الأبدان بالعبادة وطاعة النفس الشيطانية بطلب الإستعانة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the Fatiha's praise reaches its limit here, the prayer turns to direct address in Iyyaka naʿbudu wa-iyyaka nastaʿīn.
rows.anchor: ولما بلغ الثناء الغاية القصوى قال سبحانه

rows.speaker: بعض النحاة
rows.claim: Grammarians offer competing analyses of iyyāka: an independent accusative pronoun with added suffixes, a noun with attached pronouns, or a form whose support syllable carries the pronominal force.
rows.anchor: إيا في المشهور ضمير نصب منفصل واللواحق حروف زيدت لبيان الحال

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda proposed a derivation for iyyā, which al-Alusi dismisses as astonishing ignorance.
rows.anchor: وزعم أبو عبيدة إشتقاقه وهو جهل عجيب

rows.speaker: أبو الفضل الرقاشي
rows.claim: Nonstandard readings include wayyāka with waw, ʾiyyāka with a light yāʾ, ʾayyāka with a doubled yāʾ, and hiyyāka with hāʾ; the majority use the familiar form.
rows.anchor: وقد جاء وياك بقلب الهمزة واو ولا أدري أهو عن القراء أم عن العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship is the highest degree of submission and is due only to God, who bestowed the greatest gifts of life and existence; therefore prostration to another is forbidden.
rows.anchor: والعبادة أعلى مراتب الخضوع ولا يجوز شرعا ولا عقلا فعلها إلا لله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship may mean submission, obedience, supplication, or affirming God's oneness; the meanings are close, and references to worshipping idols report the opponents' claim sarcastically.
rows.anchor: وقيل لا تستعمل إلا في الخضوع له سبحانه وما ورد من نحو قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: بعض المحققين
rows.claim: A scholar distinguishes three levels: worship from hope or fear, devotion through honor or accepting duties, and pure service recognizing God's intrinsic right; the first is spiritually lowest and the last highest.
rows.anchor: وذكر بعض المحققين أن لها ثلاث درجات لأنه إما أن يعبد الله تعالى رغبة في ثوابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prayer would be invalid if the worshipper explicitly prayed for reward or the prestige of worship, since its intention must be directed to God Himself.
rows.anchor: وإليه الإشارة بقول المصلي أصلي لله تعالى فإنه لو قال أصلي لثوابه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istiʿāna means seeking assistance, and the yāʾ in its verb comes from a root wāw.
rows.anchor: والإستعانة طلب المعونة وياء فعله منقلبة عن واو

rows.speaker: الجبرية
rows.claim: The Jabriyya argue that if humans acted independently, asking God for help with action would have no point.
rows.anchor: أما الجبرية فقالوا لو كان العبد مستقلا لما كان للإستعانة على الفعل فائدة

rows.speaker: القدرية
rows.claim: The Qadariyya argue that asking help makes sense only if a person already has the capacity to perform the act.
rows.anchor: وأما القدرية فقالوا السؤال إنما يحسن لو كان العبد متمكنا في أصل الفعل

rows.speaker: ناصر الملة والدين البيضاوي
rows.claim: Al-Bayḍāwī distinguishes necessary assistance, without which action cannot occur, from nonessential help that makes an already possible act easier; neither category entails compulsion or denies capacity.
rows.anchor: قال وهي إما ضرورية أو غيرها والضرورية ما لا يتأتى الفعل دونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi reads the verse as affirming human capacity that has real effect only by God's permission, rejecting compulsion, inert capacity, and independent human control alike.
rows.anchor: وعندى أن الآية إن إستدل بها على شيء من بحث خلق الأفعال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase Iyyaka naʿbudu entails that acts issue from people through an effective capacity; saying capacity is only nominal or equivalent to none contradicts necessity and reason.
rows.anchor: إياك نعبد مشير إلى صدور الفعل من العباد وذلك يستدعي قدرة يكون بها الإيجاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iyyaka nastaʿīn denies independence: human capacity and action depend on God's permission and aid, yielding neither compulsion nor delegation of control.
rows.anchor: وقوله وإياك نستعين يدل على نفي الإستقلال فيه وأنه بإذن الله تعالى

rows.speaker: إبن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās glosses the fronted object as meaning that we worship no one besides You, repudiating idolatry and implicitly addressing polytheists.
rows.anchor: قال إبن عباس رضي الله تعالى عنهما معناه لا نعبد غيرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting You reflects God's precedence over worshippers and worship in existence, and immediately directs the worshipper's attention toward the true object of devotion.
rows.anchor: وتقديم ما هو مقدم في الوجود فإنه تعالى مقدم على العابد والعبادة ذاتا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The early explicit focus on God strengthens monotheism and guards against distraction, satanic whispering, and the thought that worship might be meant for someone else.
rows.anchor: والتصريح من أول وهلة بأن العبادة له سبحانه فهو أبلغ في التوحيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spiritual aspirant should regard God first and worship only as a vehicle toward Him, remaining absorbed in the vision of divine majesty and beauty.
rows.anchor: والإشارة إلى حال العارف وأنه ينبغي أن يكون نظره إلى المعبود أولا وبالذات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The cited contrasts distinguish the believers' remembrance of God and the Prophet's assurance of God's presence from Israel's remembrance of favors and Moses' assurance that his Lord will guide him.
rows.anchor: وكم من فرق بين قوله تعالى للمحمديين

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The plural naʿbudu can humbly join one's deficient worship to that of all worshippers instead of presenting one's own worship as worthy of mention.
rows.anchor: فقد قيل هو الإشارة إلى حال العبد كأنه يقول إلهي ما بلغت عبادتي

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another explanation says the singular would risk a false claim of exclusive devotion, since people often submit to worldly powers and seek help from powerless creatures; the plural can include the righteous.
rows.anchor: وقيل النكتة في العدول إلى الأفراد التحرز عن الوقوع في الكذب

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A further explanation hears the plural as saying that the speaker is one servant among God's servants; a humble collective identity is contrasted with the singular claims of Ishmael and Moses.
rows.anchor: وقيل لو قال إياك أعبد لكان ذلك بمعنى أنا العابد

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: The plural pronouns may include the reciter, guardian angels, and those present in congregational prayer.
rows.anchor: وقيل الضمير في الفعلين للقاري ومن معه من الحفظة وحاضري الجماعة

rows.speaker: الغزالي
rows.claim: The plural may evoke congregational prayer, which al-Ghazali says is superior to an individual's prayer.
rows.anchor: وقيل هو من باب صلاة الجماعة تفضل صلاة الفذ على ما ذكره الغزالي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reason to mention worship first is that it is a trust God offered to the heavens, earth, and mountains, so its discharge takes priority.
rows.anchor: الأول أن العبادة أمانة كما قال تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saying I worship might sound self-congratulatory; immediately asking for help shows that worship itself depends on God's enabling and permission.
rows.anchor: أنه لما نسب المتكلم العبادة إلى نفسه أوهم ذلك تبجحا وإعتدادا منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship brings the servant near to God, whereas requesting assistance does not itself do so, making worship more important.
rows.anchor: أن العبادة مما يتقرب بها العبد إلى الله تعالى والإستعانة ليست كذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship is a means, so it properly precedes the request for a need and may make that request more readily answered.
rows.anchor: أنها وسيلة فتقدم على طلب الحاجة لأنه أدعى للإجابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Offering what the Master requires before asking what one wants from Him better demonstrates sincere servitude.
rows.anchor: تقديم العبد ما يريده مولاه منه أدل على صدق العبودية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship is an unavoidable duty and the stated purpose for creating humans and jinn, so it deserves precedence.
rows.anchor: أن العبادة واجبة حتما لا مناص للعباد عن الإتيان بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship suits the preceding mention of recompense, while seeking help connects more directly with the coming request for guidance.
rows.anchor: أنها أشد مناسبة بذكر الجزاء والإستعانة أقوى إلتئاما بطلب الهداية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islam begins by singling God out in worship and escaping shirk; explicit dependence on His aid comes after monotheism is established.
rows.anchor: أن مبدأ الإسلام التخصيص بالعبادة والخلوص من الشرك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Placing nastaʿīn second preserves the cadence of the verse endings.
rows.anchor: أن في تأخير فعل الإستعانة توافق رؤوس الآي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When two actions are linked, their order can sometimes be reversed, as with fulfilling a right and then showing kindness, or the reverse.
rows.anchor: أن أحدهما إذا كان مرتبطا بالآخر لم يختلف التقديم والتأخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the mystic's journey, worship marks the end of the station of seekers; after the heart is purified by praise, the soul turns to request spiritual empowerment.
rows.anchor: أن مقام السالكين ينتهي عند قوله إياك نعبد وبعده يطلب التمكين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation of the shift to direct address is that divine attributes made God a particular known reality, moving the worshipper from proof and thought to immediate witnessing.
rows.anchor: حقيقة العبادة إنقياد النفس الأمارة لأحكام الله تعالى وصورته وقالبه الإسلام ومعناه وروحه الإيمان ونوره ونوره الإحسان وفي نعبد والإلتفات تتم الأمور الثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is spiritual progress from Islam through accepted praise to ihsan, worshipping as if one sees God; the verse's worship and address bring together these levels.
rows.anchor: ترقى بذريعة الحمد المستجاب لمزيد النعم إلى رتبة الإحسان وهو أن تعبد الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since past and future are alike to God, who owned all ages eternally, the shift from third person to direct address is fitting.
rows.anchor: لما تبين أنه ملك في الأزل ما في أحايين الأبد علم أن الشاهد والغائب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A structural explanation takes the first part as praise, naturally spoken about God, and the remainder as supplication, naturally spoken in His presence.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون السر أن الكلام من أول السورة إلى هنا ثناء والثناء في الغيبة أولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because worship belongs to the ever-present God, while praise can remain complete in His absence, each section receives the style suited to it; Abraham rejects what sets.
rows.anchor: وكانت العبادة إنما يستحقها الحاضر الذي لا يغيب كما حكى سبحانه عن إبراهيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The worshipper imitates the faithful community in its speech and hopes that joining its worship will count him among the righteous.
rows.anchor: فالعابد لما رام ذلك سلك مسلك القوم في الذكر ومزج عبادته بعبادتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person who recognizes his distance from God through humility is especially apt to receive mercy that draws him into intimacy and direct address.
rows.anchor: من لزم جادة الأدب والإنكسار ورأى نفسه بعيدا عن ساحة القرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because worship is demanding, the beloved's presence gives the servant energy to endure hardship without fatigue, as illustrated by a poetic appeal to sing before Saʿdā.
rows.anchor: المحبوب قرن سبحانه العبادة بما يشعر بحضوره ليأتي بها العابد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Praise addresses others while the mystic sees divine virtues among them; when remembrance removes the veils and all others vanish from awareness, speech necessarily turns directly to God.
rows.anchor: وأما إذا آل أمره بملازمة الإذكار إلى إرتفاع الحجب والأستار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi's own subtle reading links the turn after Judgment Day to the believer's future delight in God's presence, direct conversation, and unveiling, a mercy paired with the preceding warning.
rows.anchor: وعندي وهو من نسائم الأسحار أن الله سبحانه بعد أن ذكر يوم الدين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Sufi symbolism, Judgment Day hints at annihilating the ego's desires and attachments; once the self dies, abiding in the garden of witnessing and union follows.
rows.anchor: تلويح إلى مقام الفناء لأنه موت النفس عن شهواتها وخروجها عن جسد تعلقها بالأغيار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Beyond that union lies a station that language cannot explain; al-Alusi prays for complete absorption in witnessing God alone.
rows.anchor: وفوق هذا مقام آخر لا يفي بتقريره الكلام ولا تقدر على تحريره الأقلام

rows.speaker: الإمام السيوطي
rows.claim: Al-Suyuti, quoting Shaykh Bahāʾ al-Dīn, says there is agreement on one shift in person; al-Alusi argues that the count depends on whether one supplies the command Say and on rival definitions of iltifāt.
rows.anchor: هذا وقد ذكر الإمام السيوطي نقلا عن الشيخ بهاء الدين أنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earlier phrase al-ḥamdu lillāh itself may contain a shift depending on whether Say is supplied, so the dispute over one, two, or no shifts turns on grammatical and rhetorical assumptions.
rows.anchor: إن كان التقدير قولوا الحمد لله ففي الكلام المأمور به إلتفاتان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation for repeating Iyyaka is to specify that help is sought from God, which might remain unspecified if only one object were used.
rows.anchor: فقيل للتنصيص على طلب العون منه تعالى فإنه لو قال سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says a single object might imply that worship only draws one near when combined with asking assistance, which is not true.
rows.anchor: وقيل أنه لو أقتصر على واحد ربما توهم أنه لايتقرب إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repetition as mere emphasis is rejected because the second Iyyaka is the separate object of nastaʿīn, not a redundant object of the first verb.
rows.anchor: وفيه أن التكرير إنما يكون تأكيدا إذا لم يكن معمولا لفعل ثان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation treats the repetition as teaching believers to renew remembrance of God whenever they have a need.
rows.anchor: وقيل أنه تعليم لنا في تجديد ذكره تعالى عند كل حاجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi says the repeated object marks different grounds of relation: worship is directed to God in itself, while asking assistance depends on an attribute of His.
rows.anchor: وعندي أن التكرار للأشعار أن حيثية تعلق العبادة به تعالى غير حيثية

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some take the unexpressed object of seeking help universally, like an unrestricted verb of giving; al-Bayḍāwī's practice favors this, and it accords with a report from Ibn ʿAbbās.
rows.anchor: فقيل ليتناول كل مستعان فيه فالحذف هنا مثله في قولهم فلان يعطى

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshaf considers it better to seek God's help and enabling specifically for worship, with Guide us to the straight path explaining the requested assistance.
rows.anchor: الأحسن أن يراد الإستعانة به وبتوفيقه على أداء العبادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi prefers an unrestricted request for assistance because it unifies the surah's meaning and includes faith, worship, conduct, social dealings, salvation, and escape from every kind of error.
rows.anchor: والإنصاف عندي أن الحمل على العموم أولى ليتوافق ألفاظ هذه السورة الكريمة

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: A sound hadith to Ibn ʿAbbās commands him: when seeking help, seek God's help; al-Alusi sees it as evidence for the unrestricted reading.
rows.anchor: وقد ثبت في الصحيح عنه صلى الله تعالى عليه وسلم أنه قال لإبن عباس

rows.speaker: عبيد بن عمير الليثي وزيد بن حبيش ويحيى بن وثاب والنخعي
rows.claim: They read naʿbudu with kasra on the initial nūn, a dialect found among Qays, Tamim, Asad, Rabīʿa, and Hudhayl; the same pattern applies to nastaʿīn.
rows.anchor: وقد قرأ عبيد بن عمير الليثي وزيد بن حبيش ويحيى بن وثاب والنخعي نعبد بكسر النون

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: A few dialect forms also put kasra under the imperfect prefix in verbs such as yajillu and yaʿlamūn.
rows.anchor: على أن بعضهم قال يجل بكسر ياء المضارعة من وجل

rows.speaker: الحسن وإبن المتوكل وأبو محلف
rows.claim: They read yuʿbadu in the passive, an unusual form.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الحسن وإبن المتوكل وأبو محلف يعبد بالياء مبنيا للمفعول

rows.speaker: بعض أهل مكة
rows.claim: Some Meccans read naʿbud with a silent final dāl; the majority use the standard open nūn and damma on dāl of the Hijaz.
rows.anchor: وعن بعض أهل مكة أنه قرأ نعبد بإسكان الدال وقرأ الجمهور نعبد بفتح النون وضم الدال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Guidance is gentle direction, as suggested by the word's derivation; the related verb is also used for walking gently.
rows.anchor: الهداية دلالة بلطف لدلالة إشتقاقه ومادته عليه ولذا أطلق على المشي برفق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to lead the guilty to Hell is sarcastic, like announcing painful punishment with the wording of good news.
rows.anchor: فأهدوهم إلى صراط الجحيم ) وارد على الصحيح مورد التهكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic permits hadaa with li or ila; when used with a direct object, the verb may either describe a current state or mean bringing someone to the destination.
rows.anchor: ويقال هداه لكذا وإلى كذا فتعديه باللام وإلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When the direct-object construction means bringing someone to attainment, a verse about striving for God's paths can be understood as seeking the will to attain higher ranks or actually obtaining them.
rows.anchor: لنهدينهم سبلنا ) لسبلنا أو إلى سبلنا إلا بإرادة الإرادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Later linguists disagree whether guidance must convey the traveler to the goal or may merely point toward what will lead there.
rows.anchor: وأما باب التجوز فواسغ وهل يعتبر في الدلالة الإيصال أم لا

rows.speaker: بعض المتأخرين
rows.claim: One camp reserves guidance for direction that actually reaches the destination; another uses it for pointing to a route that can lead there.
rows.anchor: ففريق خصها بالدلالة الموصلة وآخرون بالدلالة على ما يوصل

rows.speaker: قليل
rows.claim: A third view says direct transitivity means successfully conveying and applies only to God, while constructions with li or ila mean showing a route and may describe God, the Quran, or the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وقليل قال إن تعدت إلى المفعول الثاني بنفسها كانت بمعنى الإيصال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim that guidance always conveys the recipient is contradicted by Thamud, who were shown the way yet preferred blindness; explanations involving apostasy conflict with historical and exegetical reports that most never believed.
rows.anchor: وأما ثمود فهديناهم فأستحبوا العمى على الهدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second view has difficulty with the statement that the Prophet cannot guide those he loves; explaining it as mere inability to show the way is strained.
rows.anchor: إنك لا تهدي من أحببت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The third view is unsupported by linguistic usage and is refuted by Abraham and the believing Egyptian who use direct-object guidance for human instruction.
rows.anchor: ولهذا الخلل
